> **About this vignette.** All data are simulated with `wgh_simulate()`.
> The results illustrate the code and are not research findings. The
> vignette was precomputed on a machine with
> 2 cores, so the speed-ups shown are modest. On a
> machine with 8 or 16 cores they are much larger.

The heaviest analyses of the research program are bootstraps over children,
grids of quantiles and cross-validation folds. Each replicate, quantile or
fold is independent of the others, so they can run at the same time on
several cores. The analysis code of the studies on the BMI and height-for-age
distribution [1], the pubertal velocity distribution [2] and spurt duration
[3] did this with the `future` and `furrr` packages. WeGrowHealthR builds the
same approach into its functions: you set up workers once, and every heavy
step uses them.

## What runs in parallel

| Function | What is split across workers |
|---|---|
| `wgh_rq()` | Bootstrap replicates over children |
| `wgh_lqmm()` | The quantile grid and the bootstrap replicates |
| `wgh_sitar_ci()` | Bootstrap refits of the SITAR model |
| `wgh_scalar_quantiles()` | Bootstrap replicates |
| `wgh_mediation()` | Bootstrap replicates |
| `wgh_link_outcome()` | Bootstrap replicates |
| `wgh_cluster_stability()` | Bootstrap refits of the mixture model |
| `wgh_benchmark()` | Cross-validation folds of every model |
| `wgh_condref_cv()`, `wgh_condref_compare()` | Cross-validation folds |
| Flows | Every one of the steps above inside them |

Lighter steps, such as a bootstrap of a mean, stay sequential because
sending the work to other processes would cost more than it saves.

## Setting up workers

`wgh_parallel()` starts the workers with `future::plan()`:

* `workers` is the number of R processes. The default leaves one core free
  for the rest of the computer.
* `strategy = "multisession"` (default) starts separate R sessions and works
  on every platform. `"multicore"` forks the current session, which starts
  faster but is not available on Windows or inside RStudio.
* `max_size` raises the limit on the data that can be sent to each worker
  (2 GB by default, against 500 MB in `future`), because growth data and
  fitted models are often large.

All arguments are checked before anything changes, so a wrong call leaves
your set-up as it was. `wgh_parallel_info()` shows the current state.


```r
library(WeGrowHealthR)
wgh_parallel_info()
#> # A tibble: 1 x 5
#>   plan       workers cores globals_max_size_gb parallel_active
#>   <chr>        <int> <int>               <dbl> <lgl>          
#> 1 sequential       1     2                 0.5 FALSE
old <- wgh_parallel(workers = 2)
#> Parallel plan: "multisession" with 2 workers.
wgh_parallel_info()
#> # A tibble: 1 x 5
#>   plan         workers cores globals_max_size_gb parallel_active
#>   <chr>          <int> <int>               <dbl> <lgl>          
#> 1 multisession       2     2                   2 TRUE
```

`parallel_active = TRUE` means the package will use the workers. The
function returns the previous plan invisibly, and `wgh_parallel(1)` returns
to sequential processing and restores the memory limit.

## Example: a cluster bootstrap of quantile regression


```r
wgh_config("analysis")
#> WeGrowHealthR run mode: analysis
v <- wgh_simulate(30000, seed = 2026)$visits
girls <- v[v$sex == "Female" & v$age >= 5 & v$age <= 18.5, ]
f <- haz ~ splines::ns(age, knots = c(8, 11, 14), Boundary.knots = c(5, 18.5)) * baz

t_par <- system.time(
  fit_par <- wgh_rq(girls, f, taus = c(0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.95), anchor_ages = c(6, 9, 12, 15), B = 200)
)
wgh_parallel(1)
#> Parallel plan: "sequential" with 1 worker.
t_seq <- system.time(
  fit_seq <- wgh_rq(girls, f, taus = c(0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.95), anchor_ages = c(6, 9, 12, 15), B = 200)
)
rbind(parallel = t_par, sequential = t_seq)[, "elapsed"]
#>   parallel sequential 
#>     47.602     77.253
all.equal(fit_par$slopes, fit_seq$slopes)
#> [1] TRUE
```

The two runs give **identical** results. Every replicate draws its random
numbers from its own stream (L'Ecuyer-CMRG), derived from the function's
`seed` argument, so it does not matter which worker runs which replicate, or
how many workers there are. Your own random number stream is not changed by
the call either.

## Example: a SITAR bootstrap and a linear quantile mixed model

SITAR refits and linear quantile mixed models are slow, so they gain the
most.


```r
wgh_config("dev")
#> WeGrowHealthR run mode: dev
boys <- v[v$sex == "Male" & v$age >= 6 & v$age <= 18, ]
fit <- wgh_fit_sitar(boys, df = 5, age_range = c(6, 18))
#> SITAR fitted to a random 1000 of 3643 children (run mode "dev").
wgh_parallel(2)
#> Parallel plan: "multisession" with 2 workers.
t_par <- system.time(ci_par <- wgh_sitar_ci(fit, B = 8))
wgh_parallel(1)
#> Parallel plan: "sequential" with 1 worker.
t_seq <- system.time(ci_seq <- wgh_sitar_ci(fit, B = 8))
rbind(parallel = t_par, sequential = t_seq)[, "elapsed"]
#>   parallel sequential 
#>    208.537    365.724
all.equal(ci_par, ci_seq)
#> [1] TRUE
```


```r
set.seed(1)
small <- girls[girls$pid %in% sample(unique(girls$pid), 500), ]
wgh_parallel(2)
#> Parallel plan: "multisession" with 2 workers.
t_par <- system.time(lq_par <- wgh_lqmm(small, f, taus = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9), anchor_ages = c(9, 12), B = 4))
wgh_parallel(1)
#> Parallel plan: "sequential" with 1 worker.
t_seq <- system.time(lq_seq <- wgh_lqmm(small, f, taus = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9), anchor_ages = c(9, 12), B = 4))
rbind(parallel = t_par, sequential = t_seq)[, "elapsed"]
#>   parallel sequential 
#>      2.717      2.907
all.equal(lq_par$slopes, lq_seq$slopes)
#> [1] TRUE
```

## Example: cross-validation of prediction models


```r
pc <- wgh_prediction_cohort(wgh_simulate(8000, seed = 4)$visits)
wgh_parallel(2)
#> Parallel plan: "multisession" with 2 workers.
t_par <- system.time(bm_par <- wgh_benchmark(pc, models = c("M1", "M5", "M7", "M8"), folds = 5))
wgh_parallel(1)
#> Parallel plan: "sequential" with 1 worker.
t_seq <- system.time(bm_seq <- wgh_benchmark(pc, models = c("M1", "M5", "M7", "M8"), folds = 5))
rbind(parallel = t_par, sequential = t_seq)[, "elapsed"]
#>   parallel sequential 
#>      6.671      2.928
all.equal(bm_par$performance, bm_seq$performance)
#> [1] TRUE
```

For this small cohort (a few hundred children) the parallel benchmark is
slower: sending the folds to other processes costs more than fitting them.
The small quantile mixed model above gains almost nothing for the same
reason. Parallel processing
pays off when each task takes seconds or more, as for the quantile
regression bootstrap and the SITAR refits, where the time fell by about 40% with
two workers. The results are identical in every case.

## Whole flows

The flows call these functions, so a parallel plan speeds up a whole study.
With your own data in publication mode:


```r
wgh_parallel(workers = 8)
wgh_config("publication")
rep <- wgh_flow_distributional_height(mydata)     # quantile grid and bootstrap on 8 workers
spurt <- wgh_flow_pubertal_spurt(mydata)          # SITAR bootstrap intervals on 8 workers
wgh_parallel(1)
```

## Good practice

* **Memory.** Each worker holds its own copy of the data it needs. Before a
  large run, check that the number of workers times the size of the data
  fits in memory. The package sends each worker only the objects a task
  uses, which avoids the "globals too large" error the original scripts met
  when a helper function carried its whole environment to every worker.
* **One level of parallelism.** Gradient boosting and random forests inside
  the package use one thread each, so they do not compete with the workers.
  If your BLAS library is multithreaded, limit it to one thread per worker
  (for example with the `RhpcBLASctl` package).
* **Installed package.** Workers load WeGrowHealthR from your library, so
  install the package rather than loading a development copy. If it is not
  installed, the package runs sequentially and says so.
* **Reproducibility.** Report the `seed` arguments you used. The number of
  workers does not need to be reported, because it does not change the
  results.
* **Clusters.** Any `future` plan works, including a plan over several
  machines (`future::plan(future::cluster, workers = ...)`), because the
  package only asks whether a parallel plan is active.


```r
wgh_parallel(1)
#> Parallel plan: "sequential" with 1 worker.
wgh_parallel_info()
#> # A tibble: 1 x 5
#>   plan       workers cores globals_max_size_gb parallel_active
#>   <chr>        <int> <int>               <dbl> <lgl>          
#> 1 sequential       1     2                 0.5 FALSE
```
